claims.text: Thermally induced local chemical heterogeneity governs premelting and melting in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
The relevant chemical heterogeneity includes variations in atomic ordering in the nanoparticle core.
Lower-melting constituents segregate modestly, especially at nanoparticle surfaces.
Local chemical heterogeneity creates spatial variations in bonding strength and phase-transition energy barriers.
Rapidly cooled Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles can begin as a nominally homogeneous solid solution.
The proposed intervention is incremental inert-atmosphere heating from the onset of premelting through complete melting.
Using particles of uniform size under identical inert conditions is intended to isolate thermal effects on local chemical configuration.
During heating, limited atomic mobility promotes enhanced local ordering in some regions.
During heating, atomic mobility permits slight segregation of lower-melting elements at the surface.
Regions with stronger local ordering have higher cohesive energy.
Strongly ordered regions melt more abruptly and at higher temperatures.
Segregated regions have lower local energy barriers for the phase transition.
Segregated regions initiate premelting over an extended temperature range.
Slower or controlled heating favors enhanced atomic ordering.
Particles with enhanced atomic ordering will have a sharper melting transition at a relatively higher temperature.
Particles with more pronounced local segregation will show an earlier premelting onset and a broader melting interval.
The baseline consists of rapidly cooled particles having a nominally uniform elemental distribution.
The proposed scope is nanoscale Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu under inert conditions from initial surface softening to complete liquefaction.
The behavior may differ in bulk material or when particle size or external pressure dominates.
The relative contributions of internal ordering and surface segregation, and their dependence on particle size and heating rate, remain quantitatively undetermined.
